questions.q: What does Mara use to trace each of the 5 accounts back to the event that created its access?
options: A guess based on job title
Microsoft Entra ID sign-in and audit logs, and AWS CloudTrail events, filtered to the OT/SCADA boundary's admin role and policy
A survey sent to each account holder
The compliance audit's own report
questions.explain: Mara pulls each account's real access history from Entra ID audit logs and AWS CloudTrail, looking for the specific event where each direct grant was created.

questions.q: What incident do all 5 accounts' direct grants trace back to?
options: A phishing campaign against the finance team
The Substation 12 outage, fourteen months earlier
The original zero-trust segmentation pilot rollout
A routine quarterly access review
questions.explain: All 5 accounts' direct, individually-assigned admin access was created on the same date, fourteen months earlier, during the Substation 12 outage.

questions.q: What does Hartwell's break-glass procedure require after an emergency grant, that didn't happen for these 5 accounts?
options: A second emergency grant to a backup account
Review and revocation of the emergency access within 72 hours of the incident's resolution, confirmed by a closed follow-up ticket
Immediate termination of the responders' employment
A public disclosure to customers
questions.explain: The procedure requires the emergency access to be reviewed and revoked within 72 hours of resolution -- the incident ticket was closed as resolved, but no follow-up revocation ticket was ever opened.

questions.q: Which risk register row from Lesson 10 named this exact structural weakness before anyone knew it had already happened?
options: R-01, the flat network path risk
R-03, which flagged that break-glass access has no automatic expiration
R-04, the automation single-point-of-failure risk
R-05, the audit cadence risk
questions.explain: R-03 named, as a general risk, that break-glass access has no automatic expiration and relies on manual revocation -- exactly the gap that let these 5 grants stand for fourteen months.

questions.q: Why does this lesson frame the outcome as "a sequence of individually reasonable actions" rather than a single mistake?
options: Because granting the emergency access was correct, closing the resolved outage ticket was correct, and no step in the process forced the separate revocation step to happen -- the gap is structural, not a single person's error
Because nobody can be held responsible for anything at Hartwell
Because the audit team caused the problem
Because the automation script has a bug
questions.explain: Each individual action in the sequence was reasonable at the time it happened; the failure is that the process never forced the revocation step, which is a structural gap rather than one person's mistake.
